concepts.name: Lambda's 15-minute limit vs long agent runs
Cold starts and how to reduce them
Lambda vs ECS Fargate vs App Runner vs EC2
Containers as the unit of deployment

questions.prompt: An agent run makes many tool calls and sometimes takes 25 minutes. What happens if it runs inside one invocation of a standard Lambda function?

choices.text: Lambda extends the timeout while the function is waiting on network calls
Lambda pauses the run and resumes it in a fresh execution environment
The invocation is stopped at its timeout, which can be at most 900 seconds
It finishes, but every second after 15 minutes is billed at a higher rate

questions.explanation: A standard Lambda function's timeout can be set to at most 900 seconds (15 minutes); when it's reached, the invocation ends. Waiting on the network still counts. (As of 2026 AWS also offers Lambda durable functions and Lambda Managed Instances with longer limits, but they are different programming models, not a longer timeout for a normal handler.)

questions.prompt: Which of these workloads is the best fit for a standard Lambda function?

choices.text: A webhook handler that validates a payload and puts a job on a queue in under a second
An agent loop that can run for up to 40 minutes per request
A server that holds WebSocket connections open for hours
A process that must keep an in-memory cache alive indefinitely between requests

questions.explanation: Lambda is designed for short-lived tasks that don't rely on state between invocations. A 40-minute agent loop exceeds the 15-minute limit, a long-lived connection server doesn't fit the request-by-request model, and Lambda terminates execution environments every few hours, so an in-memory cache can't be relied on. A quick webhook that hands work to a queue is the classic fit.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise: write the decision for where `agent-api` should run. Should it be a standard Lambda function or a container service such as ECS Fargate? Give your reasons.

model_answer.summary: Run `agent-api` as a container service such as ECS Fargate, because agent runs and streamed responses can outlast Lambda's 15-minute limit and the app is already a long-running web server in a container.
key_points: A standard Lambda invocation can run for at most 15 minutes, and a long agent run with many tool calls can exceed that
Fargate runs your container without you managing servers, and a service's tasks keep running with no per-request time limit
The existing Docker image (a FastAPI or similar web server) runs on Fargate as it is, while Lambda needs the Lambda runtime interface
Lambda still suits short side jobs, such as a webhook that enqueues work
The trade-off: a Fargate service costs money while its tasks run even when idle, while Lambda bills per use

questions.explanation: A good decision names the constraint that settles it (run length) and the cost of the choice (paying for idle tasks). Lambda's quotas page gives the 900-second maximum; the Fargate docs describe running containers without managing EC2 instances. Mentioning that Lambda remains useful for short event-driven pieces shows you understand where each fits.

questions.prompt: What is a Lambda cold start?

choices.text: The time your handler spends reconnecting to the database on every single call
Lambda downloading your code into a new environment and running code outside the handler
The delay while Lambda restores the function's `/tmp` directory from its backup copy in S3
The extra time the first invocation of each day spends compiling your handler code

questions.explanation: When no warm environment is available, Lambda downloads the code, starts an execution environment, and runs the initialisation code outside your handler before the handler runs. That extra latency is the cold start, and you are billed for it. Later requests can reuse the environment (a warm start), which is why connections created at module level survive between calls.

questions.prompt: A user-facing Lambda function must start quickly on every request. Which change most directly removes cold starts from the request path?

choices.text: Raise the function timeout to the 900-second maximum
Move all imports inside the handler so they run on every call
Set reserved concurrency so the function always has capacity
Configure provisioned concurrency so environments are initialised in advance

questions.explanation: AWS recommends provisioned concurrency when you need predictable start times: Lambda initialises that many execution environments ahead of requests. Reserved concurrency only caps or guarantees how many can run; it doesn't pre-warm them. Moving imports into the handler makes every warm call slower, and the timeout has nothing to do with start-up.

questions.prompt: It's 2026 and you're setting up a new AWS account. You want App Runner-style simplicity: give AWS a container image and get an HTTPS URL with load balancing and auto scaling. What does AWS recommend?

choices.text: AWS App Runner, since it's the newest and simplest container service
Amazon ECS Express Mode, which provisions a Fargate service, load balancer and scaling for you
Lambda function URLs, because App Runner was merged into Lambda
EC2 with an Auto Scaling group, since AWS has no managed option for containers

questions.explanation: AWS closed App Runner to new customers (from 30 April 2026); existing customers can keep using it, but no new features are planned. AWS points to ECS Express Mode instead: one call with a container image and two IAM roles creates an ECS service on Fargate, an Application Load Balancer, auto scaling and a URL. This is a recent change, so older tutorials still recommend App Runner.

questions.prompt: Which AWS compute option gives you the most control (choice of instance type, custom drivers, SSH access) but makes you responsible for patching the operating system?

choices.text: ECS on Fargate
AWS Lambda
Amazon EC2
ECS Express Mode

questions.explanation: EC2 gives you virtual machines, so you choose the instance type and control everything on it, and under the shared responsibility model you patch the guest operating system. Fargate, Express Mode (which runs on Fargate) and Lambda hide the servers, trading control for less work.

questions.prompt: Compare Lambda, ECS on Fargate and EC2 for hosting an agent API. Cover time limits, what you manage yourself, and how you pay when there is no traffic.

model_answer.summary: Lambda is serverless and billed per use but limited to 15 minutes per invocation; Fargate runs containers without servers to manage and without a request time limit, but you pay while tasks run; EC2 gives full control, but you manage and pay for the instances.
key_points: A standard Lambda invocation runs for at most 15 minutes; Fargate tasks and EC2 instances have no such per-request limit
With Lambda and Fargate you don't manage servers; with EC2 you manage and patch the operating system
Lambda is billed for the time your code runs, so no traffic costs close to nothing
A Fargate service keeps its desired number of tasks running, so you pay for them even when idle
EC2 instances are billed while they run, whether or not they receive traffic

questions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear that the choice follows from the workload: run length, how much control you need, and the shape of your traffic. Long agent runs rule out standard Lambda; low ops effort favours Fargate over EC2; spiky, short work favours Lambda.

questions.prompt: Why is a container image a good unit of deployment for `agent-api`?

choices.text: Code inside a container runs noticeably faster than on a plain virtual machine
A container platform doesn't need health checks, because images can't crash
Secrets baked into an image are encrypted, so they're safe to ship with it
The same image, built once, runs in CI, staging and production, so you ship what you tested

questions.explanation: An image packages the code with its runtime and dependencies. Build it once, tag it, and run the identical artefact everywhere, changing only configuration through environment variables. Most platforms (Fargate, Railway, Fly.io, and Lambda via container images) accept it. Containers don't make code faster, and secrets in an image are readable by anyone who can pull it.

questions.prompt: You want to run your existing `agent-api` Docker image (a FastAPI app started by `uvicorn`) as a Lambda function from a container image. What does Lambda require?

choices.text: Nothing: any Linux image under 10 GB runs unchanged, since Lambda forwards HTTP requests to it
It must implement the Lambda Runtime API, as AWS base images or a runtime interface client do
The image must first be exported and converted into a .zip deployment package
The image must be a multi-architecture build covering both x86_64 and arm64

questions.explanation: Lambda talks to your code through the Lambda Runtime API. AWS base images include a runtime interface client; with any other base image you must add one. A plain web server image that just listens on a port doesn't implement it. Lambda images must be Linux and at most 10 GB uncompressed, and Lambda does not support multi-architecture images: you build for one architecture.

questions.prompt: Explain what "build once, deploy the same image everywhere" means, and what should differ between the staging and production copies of `agent-api`.

model_answer.summary: You build one image per commit and promote that exact image from test to staging to production; only configuration, supplied at runtime, differs between environments.
key_points: The image is built once, for example tagged with the commit SHA, and never rebuilt for a later environment
Staging and production run byte-for-byte the same image, so what passed tests is what ships
Environment-specific values such as database URLs, API keys and log levels come from environment variables or the platform's secret store at runtime
Nothing environment-specific, and no secret, is baked into the image
Rolling back means running the previous image tag again

questions.explanation: Rebuilding for each environment can pull different dependency versions, so staging would no longer prove anything about production. Keeping config outside the image is what makes one image usable everywhere, and immutable tags make rollback simple.
